topic.name: The First Shifting Theorem of Laplace Transforms

question.text: Consider a function $r(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $\mathcal{L}\{r(t)\} = R(s)$ for $s>s_0.$ Suppose we wish to find $\mathcal{L}\{e^{3t} r(t)\}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.
question.explanation:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

\begin{align} \mathcal{L}\{e^{3t} r(t)\} &= \int_0^{\infty} \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{e^{-st} \cdot e^{3t} \, r(t)} \, \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{\infty} \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{e^{-(s-3)t}} \, r(t)\, \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] \end{align}

Now, recall that $\displaystyle R(s) = \int_0^{\infty} e^{-st} \, r(t)\, \textrm{d}t,$ where $s > s_0.$ Therefore, \[ \int_0^{\infty} e^{-(s-3)t} \, r(t)\, \textrm{d}t = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{R(s−3)}, \] where \[ s - 3 > s_0 \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{s > s_0 +3}. \]

question.text: Consider a function $w(t)$ such that its Laplace transform is $\mathcal{L}\{w(t)\} = W(s)$ for $s>s_0.$ Suppose we wish to find $\mathcal{L}\{e^{-6t} w(t)\}.$ Select the correct options in the reasoning below.
question.explanation:
Starting from the definition of the Laplace transform, we have

\begin{align} \mathcal{L}\{e^{-6t} w(t)\} &= \int_0^{\infty} \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{e^{-st} \cdot e^{-6t} \, w(t)} \, \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] &= \int_0^{\infty} \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{e^{-(s+6)t}} \, w(t)\, \textrm{d}t \\[5pt] \end{align}

Now, recall that $\displaystyle W(s) = \int_0^{\infty} e^{-st} \, w(t)\, \textrm{d}t,$ where $s > s_0.$ Therefore, \[ \int_0^{\infty} e^{-(s+6)t} \, w(t)\,\textrm{d}t = \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{W(s+6)}, \] where \[ s + 6 > s_0 \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad \bbox[4pt,border: 1px solid lightgray]{s > s_0 - 6}. \]

question.text: Given that \begin{align*} \mathcal L\left\{t^n\right\} &= \dfrac{n!}{s^{n+1}}, && s > 0, \end{align*} use linearity of Laplace transforms and the first shifting theorem to find the Laplace transform of $f(t) = 7t^2 + 5t^4e^{t}$ for $s > 1.$
question.explanation:
First, we apply the linearity properties of Laplace transforms:

\begin{align*} \mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\}& = \mathcal{L}\left\{ 7t^2 + 5t^4e^{t} \right\} \\[5pt] &= \mathcal{L}\left\{ 7t^2 \right\} + \mathcal{L}\left\{ 5t^4e^{t} \right\} \\[5pt] &= 7\mathcal{L}\left\{ t^2 \right\} + 5\mathcal{L}\left\{ t^4e^{t} \right\} \end{align*}

We are given that, for $s > 0,$ \begin{align*} \mathcal L\left\{t^n\right\} &= \dfrac{n!}{s^{n+1}}. \end{align*}

Therefore, we have the following: \begin{align} \mathcal{L}\left\{ t^2 \right\} &= \dfrac{2}{s^3} \\[5pt] \mathcal{L}\left\{ t^4 \right\} &= \dfrac{24}{s^5} \end{align}

The first shifting theorem states that if $\mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\} = F(s),$ then $\mathcal{L}\left\{e^{at}f(t)\right\} = F(s-a).$ Therefore, \[ \mathcal{L}\left\{ t^4e^{t} \right\} = \dfrac{24}{(s-1)^5}. \]

Therefore, the Laplace transform of $f(t)$ is

\begin{align} \mathcal{L}\left\{f(t)\right\} &= 7\mathcal{L}\left\{ t^2 \right\} + 5\mathcal{L}\left\{ t^4e^{t} \right\} \\[5pt] &= 7 \cdot \dfrac{2}{s^3} + 5 \cdot \dfrac{24}{(s-1)^5}\\[5pt] &= \dfrac{14}{s^3} + \dfrac{120}{(s-1)^5} . \end{align}

This transform is valid for $s>1.$
